issues.issue: This excludes earth movement "whether sudden or gradual," while the EARTH MOVEMENT COVERAGE endorsement (c273) buys back only "sudden earth movement" at scheduled locations. Whether a particular movement is sudden, and so restored to coverage, depends on reading the two together.

Flood is excluded here, but the FLOOD COVERAGE endorsement (c284) restores it at scheduled locations and COVERAGES E. 3. (c042) pays dry-out costs for electrical objects damaged by flood. The interaction of the exclusion with those two grants must be construed.

Fungus is excluded except where loss "from a specified peril ensues," yet the Fungus Cleanup extension (c068, c069) pays cleanup costs where fungus results from a covered loss by fire, lightning or any other insured peril. The exclusion and the extension describe overlapping but differently bounded coverage.

The one-word exclusion "Pollution." carries no ensuing-loss carve-back, yet the Pollution Cleanup Expense extension (c077-c079) pays to remove pollutants in defined circumstances. Which provision governs cleanup costs after an insured peril must be settled between them.

This excludes demolition, building-law and increased construction costs absolutely, while EXTENSIONS B. 6. (c095) grants exactly those costs when a sublimit is shown. The exclusion and the optional extension cannot both be applied literally.

The carve-back for "acts of destruction ordered by government to prevent the spread of fire" overlaps GROUP B exclusion 14. (c125), which excludes acts or decisions of any governmental body subject to an ensuing-loss proviso. Which of the two governs a government-ordered destruction is not settled by either text.

This excludes utility interruption where "the failure occurs away from the covered location," while the INTERRUPTION OF SERVICES COVERAGE EXTENSION (c296) insures precisely off-premises service interruptions at scheduled locations. The exclusion's continuing reach after the endorsement has to be construed.

"Any virus, organism or like substance that is capable of inducing disease, illness, physical distress or death" is open-ended, and "like substance" is a catch-all following broad specifics. Whether ordinary bacteria, mold or contaminants fall in is left to construction.

The exclusion reaches "any other electronic equipment, computerized equipment, or similar device" and any "change in the functionality, availability, operation, use of, accessibility to" those items, wording broad enough to catch ordinary equipment damage. The catch-all against the enumerated computer items is a general-versus-specific problem.

The provision is printed with orphan numbering ("1. 2 3.") preceding the text, so it is not clear which exclusion this sentence is or what the other numbered items are. The mechanical defect obscures the enumeration of GROUP B.

"Theft by employees" sits against the carve-back in exclusion B. 4. that acts of destruction, including vandalism, by employees are not excluded. Which rule applies where an employee both destroys and takes property must be construed between the two.

Subparagraph c. is mutilated — "any of your associates, proprietors, partners, directors, trustees, officers, _ oo or representatives voluntarily relinquishes possession of covered property with or without your" — so the class of persons and the qualifying condition are missing. The exclusion's scope cannot be determined from its own words.

This excludes "loss of use" and "indirect or remote loss" without any ensuing-loss proviso, while COVERAGES C. and D. (c031, c037) insure loss of business income and extra expense, which are by nature indirect losses of use. Whether the exclusion cuts into those grants is a genuine conflict.

The exclusion covers "wear and tear, deterioration ... rust, corrosion" and "any quality in the covered property that causes it to damage or destroy itself," but pays where "a covered loss ensues," a sequence the clause does not define. Where storm damage is layered on pre-existing deterioration, what portion is excluded is exactly what the words leave open.

This excludes failure or breakdown of machinery, but COVERAGES E. 1. (c040) provides that exclusion B. 8. does not apply to losses resulting from an accident to a covered object. The two must be read together to know when machinery failure is covered.

Loss attributable to faulty "construction, workmanship or material" and to faulty "design, plan or specification" is excluded, subject to "if a covered loss ensues," with no test for separating the defect from the ensuing damage. Whether damage to the defective work itself, or to other property, is excluded is left to construction.

The exclusion of "acts or decisions, including the failure to act or decide, of any governmental employee, agent, group, organization, agency or body" overlaps GROUP A exclusion 7. (c107) on government seizure and destruction, which has its own narrower carve-back. Which exclusion governs a government-ordered loss is unresolved between them.

The list excludes "Water, land ... lawns, growing crops, or standing timber" while EXTENSIONS A. 14. (c076) grants $100,000 for loss to plants, trees and shrubs. The property-not-covered list and that extension state opposite results for the same property.

The general rule that loss "will be valued ... at replacement cost" is qualified by A. 2. (c128), which withholds replacement cost until repair or replacement actually occurs and drops to actual cash value after two years. The default and the condition state different measures of recovery for the same loss.

"We will not pay replacement cost until the lost or damaged property is actually repaired or replaced," with an actual-cash-value fallback if repairs are not made "within two (2) years after the date of the physical loss," gives no rule for a case where the insurer disputes the loss and the two years run during the dispute. What "actually repaired or replaced" requires, and when the clock starts, are both open on these words.

The alternative recovery requires that capital expenditures "were not planned as of the date of loss" and be claimed within two years, neither of which is defined or evidenced by any stated standard. Whether a given expenditure was "planned" is left to argument.

The actual cash value list is preceded by broken page and copyright text and begins at subparagraph "a." without a numbered lead-in, leaving its relationship to A. Replacement Cost unclear. The mechanical break obscures which property is valued at actual cash value.

This makes appraisal available on either party's unilateral demand, but the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (c375) replaces it with a provision under which "an appraisal will be made only if both parties agree, voluntarily," and changes the appraiser-notice period from thirty to sixty days. Whether appraisal can be compelled turns on which text governs.

Item 2. on umpire selection is left in place by the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement, which replaces only items 1. and 3. (c375, c376), so a mandatory umpire mechanism survives inside a now-voluntary appraisal. The two must be read together to know what procedure applies in Kansas.

This makes the appraisers' written agreement binding as "the amount of our payment," while the KANSAS CHANGES replacement (c376) states the same rule followed by a truncated further sentence about an appraisal award. Whether an award binds the parties in Kansas cannot be settled from this provision alone.

"Your assignment of this policy will not be valid except with our written consent" does not distinguish assignment of the policy from assignment of an accrued claim after loss. Whether a post-loss assignment of proceeds is caught is a standard construction dispute.

This preserves coverage at unbreached locations, while CONDITIONS I. (c156) makes "this entire policy" void for fraud or misrepresentation. Whether a breach amounting to fraud voids everything or only affects the location involved is a conflict between the two conditions.

The sixty-day new-policy window stated here is replaced by a ninety-day window in the KANSAS CHANGES — CANCELLATION endorsement (c381). Both texts remain in the delivered policy stating different periods.

The list of permissible cancellation grounds here is deleted and replaced by a different list in the KANSAS CHANGES — CANCELLATION endorsement (c382), including different notice periods for the same grounds. The two lists cannot both govern a Kansas cancellation.

"The terms of this insurance will not be waived, changed, or modified except by written endorsement" purports to bar any waiver, including one arising from the insurer's own claim conduct. Whether it defeats waiver or estoppel arguments is a question this wording invites.

Reducing payment "to the extent you have collected that loss from others" overlaps CONDITIONS Q. Other Insurance (c173) and X. Subrogation (c189), which allocate third-party and other-insurance recoveries differently. Which reduction applies to a recovery from a third party is unclear across the three.

This voids "this entire policy" for fraud or misrepresentation, while the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (c377) replaces Item I. with a provision that merely denies payment for the loss caused by the fraudulent act and requires restitution. The consequences of insured fraud differ sharply between the two.

The clause applies where a filing "would broaden this insurance without requiring any additional premium," without saying who determines that or how a partly premium-bearing filing is treated. Whether a given filing "broadens" the policy is left undefined.

The condition operates by reference to a loss payee "shown on the SCHEDULE OF MORTGAGE HOLDERS OR LOSS PAYEES, Form RM1102," a form that does not appear on the POLICY INDEX (Form RM0003) or in this policy. The condition's trigger cannot be located within the instrument.

Mortgage-holder payment depends on the schedule in Form RM1102, which is not among the forms listed on the POLICY INDEX or attached here. Who qualifies as a scheduled mortgage holder cannot be determined from the policy as issued.

"No person or organization, having custody of your covered property, will benefit from this policy" sits against the grants for personal property of others and installation property (c030, c072), which insure property held by or for others. How far the bailee bar cuts into those grants is left to construction.

This preserves limits after payment "except for those coverages written with an annual aggregate limit of liability or sublimits of liability," language that could be read to except every sublimited coverage in the policy. The scope of the exception may swallow the rule.

This makes the policy pure excess over "any other insurance that would apply in the absence of this policy," while Q. 2. (c174) contemplates proportionate contribution and Q. 3.-4. permit other insurance without reduction. The clauses state different results for the same overlap.

Proportionate contribution here is difficult to square with Q. 1. (c173), which makes this policy payable "only after the limits of all other applicable insurance are exhausted." Whether the insurer contributes or sits excess must be resolved between the two.

The insurer may elect to repair, rebuild or replace "within a reasonable period of time" and must notify "within sixty (60) days of our receipt of your proof of loss," without stating the consequence of failing to elect or to notify. What follows from an untimely or absent election is not addressed.

"When covered property consists of several parts, we will pay only for the lost or damaged part" gives no rule for matching or continuity where undamaged parts cannot be matched to replacements. Against the pair-or-set provision immediately above it, the boundary between a "part" and a "set" is undefined.

The three payment conditions are joined by "or" after item 2 while item 1 is stated as an independent requirement, so it is unclear whether compliance plus one of the other two, or any one alone, triggers the thirty-day duty. The conjunctions make the trigger genuinely ambiguous.

Coverage is limited to loss "as the result of a peril insured against during the policy period," leaving unclear whether the peril, the physical damage or the manifestation of damage must fall inside the period. In a claim for progressive or later-discovered damage that ambiguity is decisive.

"Covered losses will be adjusted with you" is qualified only by Condition M., but the ADDITIONAL NAMED INSURED endorsement (c260) separately provides that the insurer will adjust "only with you" and pay jointly with scheduled entities. Who the insurer must adjust and pay with is set out inconsistently across the two.

The recovery-sharing formula — "in the proportion that your deductible and any provable uninsured loss bears to the total loss less your proportion of fees and expenses" — is grammatically incomplete as a calculation, since the proportion is stated without the amount to which it applies. The division of a recovery cannot be computed from these words.

This imposes a two-year suit limitation while the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (c379) deletes Item Y. and substitutes five years from the date the physical damage occurred. Which period bars a Kansas suit is a direct conflict between the two texts as delivered.

"Within two (2) years ... or the shortest time permitted by law, whichever is greater" is self-contradictory: it selects the greater of a fixed period and the shortest legally permitted period. The formula does not yield a determinate deadline.

The required protective safeguards "include, but are not limited to" the five listed items, so the insured cannot know what else must be maintained on pain of losing coverage. The open-ended catch-all against a specific list is the defect.

Subparagraph b. requiring vacant property to be valued at the smaller of actual cash value, repair cost or selling price is printed without its letter and runs on from the list in a., obscuring whether the valuation rule is a separate consequence. It also conflicts with the replacement cost basis in VALUATIONS A. 1. (c127).

"Real property is considered vacant unless at least thirty (30) percent of the square footage is" in customary use does not say whether the test is applied building by building or across a location or the policy as a whole. On a multi-building schedule that choice determines the answer.

"Give us immediate written notice of the loss" fixes no period and, unlike the Proof of Loss item, no outer date, so timeliness is measured against an undefined word. Whether notice months after a storm is "immediate" is exactly what the term leaves open.
"As soon as possible" sets no measurable deadline for the description of the loss. Compliance can only be judged by an undefined standard.

"All reasonable steps to protect the covered property from further damage" gives no benchmark for what steps are required or who bears their cost. The extent of the duty is left to argument after the fact.
